meta.title: Order flow degraded — inventory-reservation
meta.faultOneLine: Memory leak in inventory-reservation reservation cache

diagnosis.incident_summary: Order flow has been degraded across web, mobile, POS and the partner feed since 09:52 UTC, when inventory-reservation entered an OOMKill crash loop; the first symptom was a buried P4 heap alert at 08:40.

timeline.description: heap utilisation 71.2% on inv-resv-svc, above soft threshold
GC pause p99 climbing: 40ms -> 900ms over last 10 samples
OOMKilled: container exceeded memory limit, pod inv-resv-svc-7d4f restart 1
consumer lag on inventory.reserve.req begins climbing as the consumer group falls behind (offset 8517598, lag 28 and rising)
OOMKilled: pod inv-resv-svc-7d4f restart 2, crash loop detected

hypotheses.cause: Slow memory leak in the inventory-reservation reservation cache, builds over ~90 minutes to an OOMKill crash loop

supports.why: Heap crossed 71% as a soft-threshold WARN, 72 minutes before the first restart — a gradual climb, not a step change, is the classic leak signature.
GC pause p99 climbing from 40ms to 900ms over the same window is consistent with the collector fighting a shrinking free heap, not a sudden load spike.
First OOMKill lands exactly where the heap trend was heading, with no other trigger event at that timestamp.
inventory-reservation handled 40% higher peak order volume on 2026-09-09 with heap flat under 55% — rules out volume as the trigger and points at something time-based.

contradicts.why: Consumer lag was still low (28) a minute after the first restart, briefly recovering — a hard, monotonic leak would be expected to degrade further immediately rather than dip, which is also consistent with an external saturating dependency intermittently unblocking.

hypotheses.what_would_change_this: Evidence of a recent deploy, config change, or dependency version bump to inventory-reservation around 08:00–08:40 would point at a triggered regression instead of an organic leak.

hypotheses.cause: Upstream retry storm inflating batch sizes into inventory-reservation

supports.why: Sustained 504s on the internal reserve endpoint are consistent with a backed-up caller retrying aggressively.

contradicts.why: order.enriched producer rate stayed flat at baseline (820–890 msg/min) throughout the pre-incident window — no retry storm or batch-size inflation is visible upstream.

hypotheses.what_would_change_this: A visible spike in order.enriched producer rate or batch size in the 30 minutes before 09:52 would support this instead.

ruled_out.reason: Different service (nightly-settlement-batch), no shared correlation ID with the incident, and the retry resolved on its own — an unrelated routine job blip that happened to land at the same minute as the first real symptom.
Same unrelated nightly-settlement-batch job, again with no correlation ID linking it to inventory-reservation.

checks.action: Pull the inv-resv-svc deploy/rollout history for the last 7 days
checks.if_result_a: No changes in the window — supports the organic leak hypothesis
checks.if_result_b: A change lands between 07:00–08:40 — supports a triggered regression instead

checks.action: Chart heap utilisation for inv-resv-svc across the full pre-incident window
checks.if_result_a: Monotonic, roughly linear climb from ~44% to OOM — confirms a leak signature
checks.if_result_b: A step change coincides with a specific event — points at a trigger, not a leak

checks.action: Compare inventory.reserve.req producer vs. consumer throughput, today vs. 2026-09-09
checks.command: Kafka consumer-group describe + producer rate metrics, both dates, 08:00–10:00 window
checks.if_result_a: Today's producer rate is at or below last Tuesday's — rules out volume as the trigger
checks.if_result_b: Today's rate is materially higher — reopens the volume/retry-storm hypothesis

recovery.proposal: Roll inv-resv-svc pods on a staggered schedule with the memory limit raised from 768Mi to 1.5Gi to buy headroom and drain the Kafka backlog without a full outage; capture a heap dump on the next OOM before the rollout completes, to confirm the leaking object graph for a permanent fix.
recovery.risk: A larger memory limit only delays the next OOM if the leak is unbounded — if the leak rate is fast enough, pods could still exhaust the new limit within a few hours.
recovery.rollback: Revert the memory limit to the 768Mi baseline; this returns the service to its current (degraded but familiar) crash-loop behaviour with no other state mutated.

diagnosis.post_incident_note: INC0098451 — root cause: slow heap leak in inv-resv-svc reservation cache, first symptom 08:40, first OOMKill 09:52. No deploy or config change in the preceding 30 days (confirmed via late evidence at 10:24). Mitigated via staggered pod restart with raised memory limit once approved. Follow-up: heap dump analysis to identify and patch the leaking allocation path; consider a scheduled restart policy as a stopgap.

diff.changed_summary: The deploy/config history check closes the one open question against the leak hypothesis — no change to inventory-reservation in 30 days — so the memory-leak diagnosis stands confirmed rather than merely favoured, and the retry-storm alternative is now effectively closed out.

what_changed: The pod-eviction record shows no memory-limit change and no deploy to inventory-reservation in the last 30 days — this was hypothesis 1's stated 'what would change this' trigger for a lower confidence read, and it has now been resolved in the leak's favour.
Hypothesis 2 (retry storm) had no plausible remaining trigger event even before this evidence; it stays ranked 2 but is now considered closed rather than merely unlikely.

diagnosisAfterOverrides.incident_summary: Order flow has been degraded across web, mobile, POS and the partner feed since 09:52 UTC due to a confirmed memory leak in inventory-reservation; deploy history rules out any recent change as the trigger.

1.what_would_change_this: Nothing outstanding — deploy/config history confirms no trigger other than the leak itself. A heap dump would still be needed to identify the exact leaking allocation for a permanent code fix.
